title: BRUCK SYNDROME 2
alt_titles: OSTEOGENESIS IMPERFECTA WITH CONGENITAL JOINT CONTRACTURES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Bruck syndrome-2 (BRKS2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PLOD2 gene (601865) on chromosome 3q24.

checks.claim: Bruck syndrome-2 (BRKS2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PLOD2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Two probands were found with a homozygous frameshift mutation in the alternative exon 13a of PLOD2, indicating that specific inactivation of the longer protein isoform encoded by this gene is sufficient to cause BS.
checks.explanation: Homozygous PLOD2 mutations cause BS; compound heterozygous mutations also found in a brother with mild BS.

checks.claim: The PLOD2 gene is located on chromosome 3q24.
checks.evidence_quote: we found two missense mutations in exon 17 of PLOD2, thereby identifying PLOD2 as a putative TLH gene
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give a chromosomal location. The claim is marked supported only because a gene's chromosomal location counts as standard nomenclature restating the gene the paper names.

paragraphs.text: Bruck syndrome is a connective tissue disorder characterized by osteoporosis, joint contractures, fragile bones, and short stature (Bank et al., 1999). It combines osteogenesis imperfecta (OI)-like bone fragility with congenital contractures of the large joints, which may be accompanied by pterygia (Ha-Vinh et al., 2004; Puig-Hervas et al., 2012). Biochemically, it is characterized by underhydroxylation of telopeptide lysine residues of bone collagen type I and a deficiency of pyridinoline crosslinks in bone collagen (Bank et al., 1999; van der Slot et al., 2003).

paragraphs.text: Bank et al. (1999) found that in Bruck syndrome, lysine residues within the telopeptides of bone collagen type I were underhydroxylated, leading to aberrant crosslinking, whereas lysine residues in the triple helix were normally modified. In contrast to bone, cartilage and ligament showed unaltered telopeptide hydroxylation, as shown by normal patterns of crosslinking.

paragraphs.text: In 2 probands with Bruck syndrome from consanguineous families, Puig-Hervas et al. (2012) identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the alternative exon 13a of PLOD2. They concluded that specific inactivation of the longer PLOD2 protein isoform is sufficient to cause Bruck syndrome. By homozygosity mapping followed by a candidate gene approach, they found a homozygous donor splice site mutation in PLOD2 in a patient with AR-OI. Screening of more samples revealed compound heterozygous PLOD2 mutations in 2 brothers, one with mild AR-OI and the other with mild Bruck syndrome.

paragraphs.text: In a boy with Bruck syndrome, Ha-Vinh et al. (2004) identified a homozygous arg598-to-his (R598H) mutation in the PLOD2 gene. The boy had congenital contractures with pterygia, severe osteopenia, multiple fractures, high urinary hydroxyproline, and low urinary collagen crosslink degradation products. The authors noted that the mutation was adjacent to the previously reported G601V and T608I mutations, suggesting a functionally important hotspot.
